q: Normally, atoms have equal numbers of electrons and protons so the net charge on a material is zero.
e: In a neutral state, the equal number of protons and electrons results in a net charge of zero.

q: When two insulating materials are rubbed together, protons may be transferred from one to the other.
e: When two insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons may be transferred, not protons.

q: If two uncharged objects are rubbed with one another both of them become charged.
e: Rubbing two uncharged objects together causes electron transfer, leaving both objects charged.

q: Charging by rubbing is also called charging by friction.
e: The process of electrification by rubbing is commonly referred to as charging by friction.

q: Rubbing produces or creates new charges.
e: Rubbing does not produce or create charges; it only transfers existing electrons from one object to another.

q: When a glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth, the glass rod becomes positively charged.
e: The glass rod loses electrons to the silk cloth, resulting in a net positive charge on the glass rod.

q: When a glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth, the silk cloth becomes positively charged.
e: The silk cloth gains electrons from the glass rod, so it becomes negatively charged.

q: The glass rod becomes positively charged because it loses electrons.
e: The loss of negatively charged electrons leaves the glass rod with a net positive charge.

q: When a plastic rod is rubbed with fur, the plastic rod possesses a negative charge.
e: The plastic rod gains electrons from the fur, giving it a net negative charge.

q: When a plastic rod is rubbed with fur, the fur becomes negatively charged.
e: The fur loses electrons to the plastic rod, so the fur becomes positively charged.

q: Induction is the process of charging a conductor without any contact with the charged body.
e: Charging by induction involves redistributing charges in a conductor using a nearby charged object, without physical contact.

q: A charged object can attract uncharged objects.
e: A charged object can induce a charge separation in an uncharged object, leading to attraction.

q: When a negatively charged rod is placed near a metal sphere, like charges repel so electrons in the sphere move to the right side of the sphere.
e: The negative rod repels the free electrons in the metal sphere, pushing them to the far side.

q: When the sphere is touched by a wire connected to earth, electrons flow from the earth to the sphere.
e: When the sphere is earthed, electrons flow from the sphere to the earth, not from the earth to the sphere.

q: After the connection is removed and the charged object is taken away, the sphere becomes a positively charged object.
e: Because electrons flowed to the earth, the sphere is left with a deficit of electrons, making it positively charged.

q: Finally, the positive charges are uniformly distributed on the surface of the sphere.
e: Once the inducing charge is removed, the remaining positive charges spread out evenly over the sphere's surface.

q: Two metal spheres of the same size supported on insulating stands are in contact can be considered as a single conductor.
e: When in contact, the two metal spheres act together as one continuous conducting body.

q: When a negatively charged rubber rod is brought near sphere A, free electrons in both spheres move towards the rod.
e: Since like charges repel, the free electrons in both spheres move away from the negatively charged rod.

q: When a negatively charged rod is brought near, sphere A has excess positive charges, while sphere B has excess negative charges.
e: Electrons are repelled to sphere B, leaving sphere A with a deficit of electrons (positive) and sphere B with an excess (negative).

q: These excess charges on the surfaces of A and B are called induced charges.
e: The charges that appear on the surfaces of the spheres due to the nearby charged object are known as induced charges.

q: Keeping the rubber rod in position, sphere B moves slightly from sphere A, and the two spheres have opposite charges.
e: Separating the spheres while the rod is present traps the opposite charges on each respective sphere.

q: After the rubber rod is removed, sphere A becomes a negatively charged sphere.
e: After the rod is removed, sphere A remains a positively charged sphere because it lost electrons to sphere B.

q: Sphere A and B now have an equal number of opposite charges, and the magnitude of the charge on the rubber rod remains unchanged.
e: Induction does not transfer charge to or from the inducing rod, so its charge magnitude remains unchanged.

q: The law of conservation of electric charge is one of the fundamental laws.
e: The conservation of electric charge is a fundamental principle in physics.

q: The net electric charge in an isolated system remains constant.
e: This is the statement of the law of conservation of electric charge.

q: The net charge is the algebraic sum of the charges in an isolated system.
e: Net charge is calculated by adding all positive and negative charges algebraically within the system.

q: In the experiment on electrification by stroking the glass rod with a silk cloth, they together form an isolated system.
e: The glass rod and silk cloth together can be considered an isolated system where no charge enters or leaves.

q: There is charge transfer between the surrounding and the isolated system during stroking.
e: There is no charge transfer between the surrounding and the isolated system; charge is only transferred between the rod and the cloth.

q: Photocopier, electrostatic paint spraying, electrostatic precipitator etc., are based on static electric charges.
e: These are practical daily life applications that utilize the principles of static electricity.

q: Basic operation of a photocopier is the attraction of charged toner to the region on the selenium coated drum that is oppositely charged.
e: The photocopier works by using electrostatic attraction to pull charged toner onto specific oppositely charged areas of the drum.

q: In electrostatic paint spraying, the item to be painted receives the positive charge from a positively charged electrode.
e: In electrostatic paint spraying, the item to be painted receives a negative charge from a negatively charged electrode.

q: The droplets of paint emerge from the spray gun are positively charged.
e: The paint droplets are given a positive charge so they will be attracted to the negatively charged object.

q: As the paint droplets all carry the same charge they repel and spread out forming a fine spray.
e: Mutual repulsion between the positively charged droplets causes them to spread out evenly.

q: The paint is attracted statically to metal frame from every direction so there is no waste of spray paint.
e: The electrostatic attraction ensures the paint wraps around the frame, minimizing waste.

q: In an electrostatic precipitator, waste smoke, dust and fly ash are passed through a positively charged mesh of wire.
e: In an electrostatic precipitator, the waste smoke and ash are passed through a negatively charged mesh of wire.

q: In the chimney, the negatively charged fly ash particles are attracted and stick to positively charged metal plate.
e: The negatively charged ash particles are attracted to the oppositely charged (positive) collecting plates.

q: Static electricity occurs when there is an imbalance of charges between two objects.
e: An imbalance of positive and negative charges between objects is the scientific definition of static electricity.

q: Static electricity can build up as a result of collisions among the molecules in clouds.
e: Friction and collisions between molecules in clouds can generate a significant buildup of static charge.

q: A huge spark forming between the ground and the cloud causes a lightning discharge.
e: Lightning is a massive electrostatic discharge caused by the spark between a charged cloud and the ground.

q: As aircraft fly through the air, they can become charged with static electricity.
e: Friction with air molecules during flight can cause an aircraft to accumulate static electric charge.

q: A build-up of static charge is a potential danger when refuelling aircraft or vehicles.
e: Static charge buildup can create sparks, which is highly dangerous in the presence of flammable fuel.

q: Fuel running through the pipes can provide the friction needed to create a static charge.
e: The flow and friction of fuel inside pipes can generate static electricity.

q: To prevent static charge build-up, aircraft are earthed with an insulator during refuelling.
e: To prevent static charge build-up, aircraft are earthed with a conductor, not an insulator, during refuelling.

q: Fuel tankers that transport fuel on roads must be earthed before any fuel is transferred, to prevent sparks causing a fire or explosion.
e: Earthing the fuel tanker safely dissipates any static charge, preventing dangerous sparks.

q: Television screen and computer monitors become charged with static electricity when they are powered.
e: The operation of these electronic displays can lead to a buildup of static electric charge on their surfaces.

q: These static charges on screens attract dust.
e: The static charge on the screen attracts neutral dust particles from the surrounding air.
